title: XII. And There Was No Murder Either
paragraphs: “Gentlemen of the jury, I ask you to remember that a man’s life is at stake, and that you must take care. We heard the prosecutor himself admit that until today he had doubts about charging the prisoner with full and deliberate planning of the crime. His doubts lasted until he saw that fatal drunken letter, which was read out in court today. ‘All was done as written.’ But I say again: he was running to her, to look for her, for one purpose only—to learn where she was. No one can dispute that. Had she been at home, he would not have run off. He would have stayed beside her, and so would never have done what he promised in the letter. He ran on a sudden impulse, by chance, and by then he very likely no longer remembered his drunken letter. ‘He snatched up the pestle,’ they say, and you will remember how a whole edifice of psychology was built on that pestle—why he was bound to see it as a weapon, why he was bound to grab it, and so on and so on. A very ordinary thought comes to me here. Suppose that pestle had not been in view. Suppose it had not been lying on the shelf where the prisoner snatched it up, but had been put away in a cupboard. It would not have caught his eye. He would have run out without a weapon, with empty hands, and then he would certainly have killed no one. How, then, can I treat the pestle as proof of premeditation?

“Yes, but he talked in the taverns of murdering his father. And two days earlier, on the evening he wrote the drunken letter, he was quiet and did no more than quarrel with a shopman in a tavern—because a Karamazov cannot help quarreling, we are told! My answer is this. If he were planning a murder such as the letter describes, he certainly would not have quarreled even with a shopman. He would probably not have gone into the tavern at all. A man plotting such a crime wants quiet and privacy. He wants to efface himself and avoid being seen or heard, and he wants it not out of calculation but out of instinct. Gentlemen of the jury, the psychological method cuts both ways, and we can use it too. As for all this shouting in taverns through the whole month, do we not often hear children, or drunkards stumbling out of taverns, cry, ‘I’ll kill you’? Yet they murder no one. And that fatal letter—is it not simply drunken ill temper as well? Is it not just the cry of a brawler outside a tavern, ‘I’ll kill you! I’ll kill the lot of you!’ Why not? Why could it not be that? What reason do we have to call that letter ‘fatal’ and not absurd? Because his father was found murdered. Because a witness saw the prisoner running out of the garden with a weapon in his hand, and was knocked down by him. So, we are told, everything happened as he had planned in writing, and the letter was not ‘absurd’ but ‘fatal.’

“Now, thank God, we have reached the real point: ‘Since he was in the garden, he must have murdered him.’ In those few words—‘since he _was_, then he _must_’—the whole case for the prosecution rests. He was there, so he must have done it. But what if there is no _must_ about it, even if he was there? Oh, I grant that the chain of evidence and the coincidences are truly suggestive. But take these facts one by one, leaving aside how they connect. Why, for instance, does the prosecution refuse to believe the prisoner when he says he ran away from his father’s window? Remember the sarcasm the prosecutor heaped on the respectful and ‘pious’ feelings that supposedly came over the murderer all of a sudden. But what if there was something of the kind—a feeling of religious awe, if not of respect for his father? ‘My mother must have been praying for me at that moment,’ the prisoner said at the preliminary inquiry. And so he ran away as soon as he was satisfied that Madame Svyetlov was not in his father’s house. ‘But he could not have satisfied himself by looking through the window,’ the prosecutor objects. Why could he not? Why? The window opened to the signals the prisoner gave. Fyodor Pavlovitch might have spoken a word, cried out something, that told the prisoner she was not there. Why must we suppose that everything happened as we picture it, as we have resolved to picture it? A thousand things can happen in real life that the subtlest imagination misses.

“‘Yes, but Grigory saw the door open, so the prisoner was certainly inside the house, and therefore he killed him.’ Now, about that door, gentlemen of the jury.... Notice that we have the word of only one witness about that door, and at the time he was in such a state that— But suppose the door was open. Suppose the prisoner lied when he denied it, out of the instinct of self-defense that is natural in his position. Suppose he did go into the house—well, what of it? How does it follow that, because he was there, he committed the murder? He might have dashed in and run through the rooms. He might have pushed his father aside. He might have struck him. But once he had made sure that Madame Svyetlov was not there, he may have run off, glad that she was not there and that he had not killed his father. And perhaps it was exactly because he had escaped the temptation to kill his father, because his conscience was clear and he was glad he had not killed him, that he was capable of a pure feeling, of pity and compassion. That is why, a minute later, he jumped down from the fence to help Grigory, the man he had knocked down in his agitation.

“With terrible eloquence the prosecutor painted for us the dreadful state of the prisoner’s mind at Mokroe, when love lay before him once more and called him to a new life. Love was impossible for him, said the prosecutor, because behind him lay his father’s bloodstained corpse, and beyond that corpse—retribution. And yet the prosecutor still granted him love, which he explained in his own manner, speaking of the prisoner’s drunkenness, of a criminal being led to execution while it is still far off, and so on and so on. But I ask again, Mr. Prosecutor, have you not invented a new personality? Is the prisoner so coarse and heartless that at such a moment he could think of love, and of tricks to escape punishment, if his hands were really stained with his father’s blood? No, no, no! The moment it became clear to him that she loved him and was calling him to her side, promising him new happiness, oh, then, I insist, the urge to kill himself must have doubled and trebled in him. If his father’s murder had been on his conscience, he must have killed himself. Oh, no! He would not have forgotten where his pistols lay! I know the prisoner. The savage, stony heartlessness the prosecutor gives him is at odds with his character. He would have killed himself—that is certain. He did not kill himself precisely because ‘his mother’s prayers had saved him,’ and because he was innocent of his father’s blood. That night at Mokroe he was troubled and grieving only over old Grigory. He was praying to God that the old man would get well, that his blow had not been deadly, and that he would not have to pay for it. Why not accept such an explanation of the facts? What reliable proof do we have that the prisoner is lying?

“But we shall be told right away, once more, ‘There lies his father’s corpse! If he ran away without murdering him, who did murder him?’ Here, I say again, is the whole logic of the prosecution. Who murdered him, if not he? There is no one to put in his place.

“Gentlemen of the jury, is that really so? Is it positively, actually true that there is no one else at all? We watched the prosecutor count off on his fingers every person who was in that house that night. There were five of them. Three, I agree, cannot be held responsible: the murdered man himself, old Grigory, and his wife. That leaves the prisoner and Smerdyakov. And the prosecutor cries out, with great effect, that the prisoner pointed at Smerdyakov only because he had no one else to pin it on. If there had been a sixth person, he says, even the ghost of a sixth person, the prisoner would at once have dropped the charge against Smerdyakov, ashamed, and accused that other. But, gentlemen of the jury, why may I not draw the exact opposite conclusion? There are two persons—the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Why can I not say that you accuse my client simply because you have no one else to accuse? And you have no one else only because you have made up your minds to keep Smerdyakov free from all suspicion.

“It is true that Smerdyakov is accused only by the prisoner, his two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. But others accuse him as well. There are vague rumors of a question, of a suspicion, an obscure report, a sense of expectation. Finally, there is the evidence of a combination of facts that is very suggestive, though, I admit, not conclusive. First, there is the fit that struck precisely on the day of the catastrophe. For some reason the prosecutor felt he had to defend its genuineness carefully. Then there is Smerdyakov’s sudden suicide on the eve of the trial. Then there is the equally startling testimony given in court today by the elder of the prisoner’s brothers. He had believed in the prisoner’s guilt, yet today he brought out a bundle of notes and named Smerdyakov as the murderer. Oh, I fully share the conviction of the court and the prosecutor that Ivan Karamazov is suffering from brain fever. His statement may truly be a desperate attempt, hatched in delirium, to save his brother by putting the guilt on a dead man. But still, Smerdyakov’s name has been spoken, and once more there is a hint of mystery. Something is unexplained, unfinished. And perhaps one day it will be explained. But we will not go into that now. That is for later.

“The court has resolved to go on with the trial. Meanwhile, I would like to make a few remarks on the portrait of Smerdyakov that the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and talent. I admire his talent, but I cannot agree with him. I have visited Smerdyakov. I have seen him and talked with him, and he made quite a different impression on me. His health was weak, it is true. But in character, in spirit, he was far from the weak man the prosecutor has made of him. I found no sign of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. Nor was he simple. On the contrary, I found an extreme distrust, hidden behind a mask of _naïveté_, and a mind of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too simple in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me, and I came away convinced that he was a plainly spiteful creature, wildly ambitious, vengeful, and intensely envious. I made some inquiries. He resented his birth and was ashamed of it, and he would grind his teeth when he remembered that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was disrespectful to the servant Grigory and his wife, who had looked after him in his childhood. He cursed Russia and sneered at it. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often used to say that he had not the money for it. I believe he loved no one but himself, and he held a strangely high opinion of himself. His whole notion of culture came down to good clothes, clean shirt-fronts and polished boots. He believed himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son (there is evidence of this), and he might well have resented his position beside his master’s legitimate sons. They had everything, and he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he was only the cook. He told me himself that he had helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The purpose of that sum—a sum that would have made his career—must have been hateful to him. Besides, he saw three thousand roubles in new rainbow-colored notes. (I asked him about that on purpose.) Oh, beware of showing an ambitious and envious man a great sum of money all at once! And it was the first time he had seen so much money in one man’s hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may have left a morbid mark on his imagination, but with no immediate result.

“The talented prosecutor, with remarkable subtlety, set out for us all the arguments for and against the theory that Smerdyakov is guilty. In particular he asked what reason Smerdyakov could have had to fake a fit. But he may not have been faking at all. The fit may have come on quite naturally, and it may equally well have passed quite naturally. The sick man may have recovered—not fully, perhaps, but enough to regain consciousness, as happens with epileptics.

“The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it is very easy to name that moment. He might have woken out of a deep sleep (for he was only asleep—an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very moment when old Grigory shouted at the top of his voice, ‘Parricide!’ That shout in the dark and the silence may have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may by then have been lighter. He might quite naturally have woken up an hour earlier.

“Getting out of bed, he goes almost without knowing it, with no clear purpose, toward the sound, to see what is wrong. His head is still muddled from his attack, and his mind is half asleep. But once he is in the garden he goes to the lighted windows, and his master, who would of course be glad to see him, gives him terrible news. His mind starts working at once. He hears every detail from his frightened master, and little by little, in his disordered brain, an idea takes shape—a terrible one, but tempting and irresistibly logical. Kill the old man, take the three thousand, and put all the blame on his young master. A terrible greed for money, for plunder, may have gripped him as he saw that he was safe from discovery. Oh, such sudden and irresistible impulses come so often when the chance is favorable, above all to murderers who never thought of committing murder beforehand. And Smerdyakov may have gone in and carried out his plan. With what weapon? Why, with any stone picked up in the garden. But why? For what purpose? Why, for the three thousand, which means a career for him. Oh, I do not contradict myself—the money may have existed. And perhaps Smerdyakov alone knew where to find it, where his master kept it. And the wrapping that held the money—the torn envelope on the floor?

“A little while ago the prosecutor was explaining his subtle theory that only an inexperienced thief like Karamazov would have left the envelope on the floor, and that a man like Smerdyakov would have taken care not to leave evidence against himself. As I listened, I felt I was hearing something very familiar. And, would you believe it, I had heard that very argument, that very guess at how Karamazov would have behaved, from Smerdyakov himself, exactly two days before. What is more, it struck me even then. I thought there was an artificial simplicity about him. I thought he was in a hurry to plant this idea in my mind, so that I would take it for my own. He slipped it in, so to speak. Did he not slip the same idea in at the inquiry, and suggest it to the talented prosecutor?

“I shall be asked, ‘What about the old woman, Grigory’s wife? She heard the sick man groaning close by, all night long.’ Yes, she heard it, but that testimony is highly unreliable. I once knew a lady who complained bitterly that a dog in the yard had kept her awake all night. Yet it turned out that the poor creature had yelped only once or twice. And that is natural. A man who is asleep hears a groan and wakes up, annoyed at being woken, but he drops off again at once. Two hours later he hears a groan again, wakes, and drops off again. Another two hours, and the same thing—three times in all during the night. In the morning the sleeper wakes and complains that someone was groaning all night and kept him awake. And it must seem that way to him. He has no memory of the two-hour stretches of sleep in between. He remembers only the moments of waking, so he feels he was awake all night.

“But why, why, asks the prosecutor, did Smerdyakov not confess in his last letter? Why did his conscience urge him to one step and not to the other? But forgive me: conscience implies repentance, and the suicide may have felt no repentance, only despair. Despair and repentance are two very different things. Despair may be vengeful and unforgiving, and a man who lays hands on himself may well have felt his hatred double for those he had envied all his life.

“Gentlemen of the jury, beware of a miscarriage of justice! What is there in all I have just laid before you that is so improbable? Find the flaw in my reasoning. Find the impossibility, the absurdity. And if there is only a shade of possibility, only a shade of probability in what I propose, do not condemn him. And is it only a shade? I swear by everything sacred that I fully believe in the account of the murder that I have just given. What troubles me and makes me indignant is this: of the whole mass of facts the prosecution has piled up against the prisoner, there is not one that is certain and beyond refutation. And yet the unhappy man is to be ruined by the sheer weight of these facts. Yes, the effect of the pile is awful: the blood, the blood dripping from his fingers, the bloodstained shirt, the dark night ringing with the shout ‘Parricide!’, and the old man falling with a broken head. And then the mass of phrases, statements, gestures, shouts! Oh, this has so much influence, it can so sway the mind. But, gentlemen of the jury, can it sway your minds? Remember that you have been given absolute power to bind and to loose. But the greater the power, the more terrible the responsibility.

“I do not withdraw one iota of what I have just said. But suppose, for a single moment, that I agreed with the prosecution that my luckless client did stain his hands with his father’s blood. This is only a supposition, I repeat. I never doubt his innocence for one instant. But so be it: I assume that my client is guilty of parricide. Even so, hear what I have to say. I have it in my heart to say something more to you, for I feel that a great struggle must be going on in your hearts and minds.... Forgive me for speaking of your hearts and minds, gentlemen of the jury, but I want to be truthful and sincere to the end. Let us all be sincere!”

At this point the speech was broken by rather loud applause. The last words had been spoken in such a sincere tone that everyone felt he really might have something to say, and that what he was about to say would matter very much. But the President heard the applause and announced in a loud voice that he would have the court cleared if it happened again. Every sound died away, and Fetyukovitch began in a voice full of feeling, quite unlike the tone he had used until then.
